description: Literary/rhetorical devices for copy that's allowed to have personality — marketing headlines, taglines, empty states, onboarding, feature names. NOT for error messages, form fields, or system copy, where clarity beats cleverness. Pair with phonaesthetics.json: a device picks the figure of speech, phonaesthetics picks the sounds that carry it.
note_on_scope: Trimmed from a broader literary-terms list down to what earns its place in short-form product copy. Left out on purpose: idiom, invective, hyperbole, euphemism, pun, foreshadowing, oxymoron, apostrophe, symploce — either too narrative/fiction-oriented, too easy to overuse, or too risky (idiom breaks in translation, hyperbole undercuts trust, puns split a room). If a case comes up where one of these earns its place, add it deliberately rather than reaching for the full literary list by default.

devices.name: Metaphor
devices.description: States one thing is another to carry over a quality, without 'like' or 'as'.
devices.example: "Your inbox, zero." — states the goal as the state, doesn't describe getting there
devices.caution: One metaphor per surface. Mixing two in the same sentence reads as confused, not clever.

devices.name: Simile
devices.description: A lighter-touch comparison using 'like' or 'as' — commits less than a metaphor, so it's safer for copy that needs to stay literal-adjacent.
good_for: one-off comparisons in tooltips or empty states
devices.example: "Set up in minutes, not like the old way."
devices.caution: Weaker than metaphor. Use metaphor if you can commit; use simile if the comparison is a side note.

devices.name: Personification
devices.description: Gives the system, a feature, or an abstract process human agency or feeling.
good_for: error framing where a system, not the user, is at fault
devices.caution: Keep it to one beat. A whole screen of a chatty personified system reads as gimmicky.

devices.name: Epithet
devices.description: A short, descriptive nickname for a feature or concept that makes it memorable and referenceable later.
good_for: naming a feature, mode, or internal concept that needs to be talked about repeatedly
devices.caution: Once named, that name is the permanent term — see `id: consistent-terminology` in SKILL.md. Don't rename it later.

devices.name: Metonymy / Synecdoche
devices.description: Metonymy: an associated thing stands in for the whole ("the cloud" for remote servers). Synecdoche: a literal part stands in for the whole ("seats" for user licenses).
good_for: compressing a technical concept into one familiar word
devices.example: "Add more seats" instead of "add more user licenses"
devices.caution: Only works if the substitute term is already familiar to the audience. Don't invent a new one and expect it to land.

devices.name: Anaphora / Epistrophe
devices.description: Repeating the same word or phrase at the start (anaphora) or end (epistrophe) of consecutive short lines — usually a feature list or a 3-step onboarding flow.
devices.example: "No setup fees. No hidden costs. No surprises." (anaphora)
devices.caution: Needs 3 short parallel lines minimum to land. Two doesn't read as a pattern; four+ gets tedious.

devices.name: Allusion
devices.description: A brief indirect reference to something the audience already recognizes.
good_for: marketing copy for a specific, known audience
devices.caution: Audience-dependent by definition. Wrong for anything localized or for an audience you can't assume shares the reference. Skip for anything global or enterprise-formal.

devices.name: Paradox
devices.description: A statement that looks contradictory on the surface but resolves into a real insight.
good_for: a single punchy line — hero headline, section title
devices.caution: One per piece, max. It's a mic-drop device — it stops working if you keep dropping the mic.

devices.name: Anastrophe
devices.example: "Powerful, this update is." (use sparingly — very Yoda, very noticeable)
devices.caution: Extremely high-visibility device. Almost always reads as try-hard outside of one deliberate, load-bearing line.
